$comment: NV-8: one home per concept. These are the concepts the console lets an operator change from more than one place, each with the places and the reason it is still so. The list may only get shorter: styles/concept-doors.test.ts fails on a concept added, and asks for `baseline` to go down when one is removed. Edit it by hand in the change that gives a concept a single home (the others become a link, the same component filtered to that scope, or a read-only summary that says where it is managed).

doors: Logs (the sidebar: search across every application)
the build log of each deployment
concepts.reason: Each reads a different source with the same toolbar; the register folds Server > Logs into /logs?source=system and the rest are scoped views of one component.

doors: Application > Settings > Previews (the variables a preview gets)
concepts.reason: Six scopes of one idea (who sees the value, from the narrowest to the whole instance); each scope is its owner's page and none can hold the others without hiding whose value it is.
A person, what they may do, who they belong to and who must agree are four questions that grew five pages; the grouping 'People and access' puts them side by side before they are merged.

doors: the live toasts and the inbox
concepts.reason: Where the message goes, when it is sent and what is watched are separate subsections of Monitoring; each is longer than a screen on its own (NV-9).
Activity is what happened to the machine and the audit log is what was done and by whom; they cross-link instead of merging because their permissions and retention differ.
Settings > Servers redirects to Fleet > Servers once the register ships; Cloud providers and Central configure how servers come to exist and are not the list.

doors: Server > System updates (the operating system's packages)
concepts.reason: Three different things are called updates: the system's packages, Noust itself and the fleet's rollout of both; the glossary keeps them apart by name.
The host's findings, the person's sign-in and one service's hardening are three subjects that share a word; the labels differ and Settings > Security is gone.
The same terminal screen at two scopes (the machine, one application's directory); each is reached from its own header.
The first freezes the server, the second one application; the application's page shows the server's freeze as read-only when it is on.
A database's schedule is the database's own and the folder is a server setting; both link to the Backups area, which holds the policy.
Five adjacent subsections with near names; the application settings grouping (Code, Deploys, Triggers) separates them by what starts a deployment.
The area lists every name on the server; an application's tab edits its own names and the console's name is the one setting that publishes the console.
